newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania reports progress on coffee tree research.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania reports progress on coffee tree research.

text.p: Tanzania is making progress in its eforts to develop a disease-resistant coffee tree suitable for commercial planting, researchers said.

"The variety being developed...is not a dwarf type but a tall variety based on the same source of resistance. It's undergoing trials," Pierre Charmetant, a French expert, said at the weekend at the Lyamangu Agricultural Research Institute (LARI).
He told Reuters research was focusing on the development of a type of tree resistant to coffee berry disease (CBD) and leaf rust, two of the biggest problems affecting Tanzanian coffee.
"For me CBD has more impact than leaf rust. I think CBD is really the major disease (in Tanzania)," he said.
Charmetant said development of a disease-resistant Tanzanian coffee variety, first started in the 1950s, was "now at the stage of final selection".
He added, "The major characteristic it brings is its resistance (to disease)."
One possible advantage of the Tanzanian variety, developed from 16 different hybrids, was a more drought resistant root system compared with dwarf varieties.
Once commercial planting started, the variety was seen bringing a considerable increase in yields from the current national average of 200 kg per hectare.
Tanzania's production for 1996/97 is forecast at 41-43,000 tonnes, down from a 1995/96 outturn of 53,000.
LARI director Epimaki Koinange said the institute had devoted its research exclusively to coffee since 1994.
"Right now, we're trying our best to improve (Tanzanian) coffee through research. The number one problem is disease and the long-term solution to that is variety improvement," he said.

"We've had some progress in developing (disease) resistant material. We're waiting for results from trials started in 1995. We're expecting a crop this year -- this may give us a guideline when to release (in commercial quantities)."
Tanzania Coffee Association secretary Jeremy Lefroy said growers were urgently seeking disease-resistant varieties that would reduce dependency on expensive inputs.
